t: Minimum Time to Finish the Race: Bounded-Segment DP
o: Each tire's lap times grow geometrically: successive laps on the same tire cost f, f*r, f*r^2, ... with r >= 2, and switching to any tire (even the same kind) costs changeTime seconds. In the first sample we run two laps on tire 0 (2 + 6 seconds), pay 5 to change, then run two more laps fresh on tire 0 (2 + 6), totaling 21 — the optimum for numLaps = 4. numLaps is small (<= 1000) but the tire fleet is huge (up to 10^5), so per-lap reasoning must never iterate all tires repeatedly. The geometric growth is the key lever: once a tire's next lap would cost more than minF + changeTime (minF being the cheapest first lap anywhere), restarting with a fresh best tire beats continuing, which caps any usable streak at about log2(minF + changeTime) <= ~18 laps.
k: Since r >= 2, lap times grow geometrically; no tire should ever run more than roughly log2(changeTime + minF) ≈ 18 consecutive laps.
Collapse all tires into one table best[x] = minimal total time for x consecutive laps on a single tire, computed by walking each tire's prefix sums until they exceed minF + changeTime.
dp[j] = min over segment length x of dp[j - x] + changeTime + best[x], seeded with dp[0] = -changeTime so the very first tire is not charged a fake change.

a.n: Approach 1: Bottom-Up DP with Capped Segment Lengths
a.i: Precompute best[x] for x up to the cap by extending each tire's cumulative lap sum only while its next lap cost stays within minF + changeTime; longer streaks are provably suboptimal because cutting before an expensive lap and paying one change always helps. Then fill dp over lap counts, trying every capped segment length as the final stretch of the first j laps. The -changeTime seed cancels the change fee of the opening segment, so dp[numLaps] is exactly the race minimum.
s: Compute minF = smallest first-lap cost and limit = minF + changeTime.
For each tire, accumulate prefix sums of laps while the current lap cost <= limit and at most numLaps laps, recording best[x] = min prefix sum.
Initialize dp[0] = -changeTime and dp[j] = infinity otherwise.
For each j from 1 to numLaps, set dp[j] = min over x of dp[j - x] + changeTime + best[x] using finite best[x] only.
a.t: O(T * X + L * X) where T = tires.length, L = numLaps and X ≈ log2(limit) <= ~18.
a.sp: O(L) for the best-segment table and dp array.

a.n: Approach 2: Top-Down Memoized Recursion Over Remaining Laps
a.i: Define solve(j) as the minimum time to run j more laps given that the next segment starts free (no change fee attached to its beginning). Each choice consumes a capped-length streak x with cost best[x], plus changeTime followed by solve(j - x) whenever laps remain. Memoizing solve over the at most numLaps distinct states gives the same recurrence as Approach 1 in top-down form, which many find easier to derive directly from the problem statement.
s: Build the same capped best[x] table from all tires.
Define solve(j): minimum time for j remaining laps with the current segment already started.
solve(j) = min over usable x <= j of best[x] + (x < j ? changeTime + solve(j - x) : 0).
a.t: O(T * X + L * X) — identical work to the bottom-up version, organized recursively.
a.sp: O(L) memo plus O(L) recursion depth.

w: The exponential-growth observation is the whole problem: without capping streak lengths you cannot even enumerate segments efficiently, and with it both approaches are tiny despite T up to 10^5. Pitfalls: charging changeTime to the very first tire (avoid it via the dp[0] = -changeTime seed or the free-start recursion), overflowing 64-bit products like lap * r in C++/Java, and forgetting that re-using the same tire type also costs changeTime. Edge case numLaps = 1 returns the global minimum f. Follow-ups include maximizing laps under a time budget, or tires whose r can equal 1 (constant lap times), where the cap argument must be revisited.
